summary: Proverbs 23 (35 verses) continues the story of wisdom. Starting with 'When you sit to eat with a ruler, consider diligently what is before you;', it moves through themes of wisdom, fear of LORD and calls readers toward practical life.
whyItMatters: This chapter matters because it shows wisdom lived out in royal court wisdom. For a first-time reader, it answers: who is God in this moment, what does he ask, and how do people respond.

keyVerses.text: When you sit to eat with a ruler, consider diligently what is before you;
Indeed surely there is a future hope, and your hope will not be cut off.
“They hit me, and I was not hurt! They beat me, and I don’t feel it! When will I wake up? I can do it again. I will look for more.”

questions.question: What is happening in Proverbs 23?
questions.answer: In 35 verses, this chapter proverbs 23 (35 verses) continues the story of wisdom. starting with 'when you sit to eat with a ruler, consider diligently what is before you;', it moves through themes of wisdom, fear of lord and calls readers toward practical life. The setting is royal court wisdom, written to young, community. Look for who speaks, who listens, and what changes by the end.

questions.question: Who wrote Proverbs and why 23 matters in the bigger story?
questions.answer: Traditionally solomon and others, addressed to young, community around ~950-700 bc compiled. This chapter fits the book's purpose as proverbs — its themes of wisdom, fear of LORD build on what came before.

questions.question: What does 'faith' mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: Trust, loyalty to God. In this chapter, it appears in context of wisdom. For a first-time reader: think of it as trust, loyalty to god, not just religious jargon.

questions.question: What does this chapter teach about God or people?
questions.answer: Through wisdom and fear of LORD, it shows God's character (faithful, just, merciful) and human tendency (need, failure, hope). Notice how verses move from problem to provision.

questions.question: Verse 35 is long — what is it saying in plain English?
questions.answer: The verse says: '“They hit me, and I was not hurt! They beat me, and I don’t feel it! When will I wake up? I can do it again. I will look for more.”...' In plain terms: it is making a key point about wisdom. Break it into two halves — what is described, and what is promised or commanded.

questions.question: How could this chapter apply today without forcing modern ideas onto it?
questions.answer: Ask: what was original audience supposed to do with this? Then ask: what similar situation exists today? For example, if chapter warns about idols, today that might be money or status; if it celebrates deliverance, where do people need deliverance today?
